title: Enrolling your child in public school
text: Every child living in the United States has the right to a free public education from kindergarten through 12th grade, regardless of their or their parents' immigration status. The Supreme Court decided this in Plyler v. Doe (1982). Schools may not ask about immigration status and may not require a Social Security number to enroll. To register, districts usually ask for proof of the child's age (such as a birth certificate or passport), proof that you live in the district (such as a lease or utility bill), and immunization records. If you are missing a document, the school must still help you enroll, and children experiencing homelessness can enroll right away under the McKinney-Vento Act.

title: How grade levels work
text: US schools are usually divided into elementary school (kindergarten to grade 5), middle school or junior high (grades 6 to 8), and high school (grades 9 to 12). Some districts also offer free pre-kindergarten for 3- and 4-year-olds. Children are placed in a grade mainly by age; the cutoff birthday for kindergarten (often around September 1) is set by each state. Students arriving from another country are generally placed with children their own age, not held back because they are still learning English. High school students earn credits in each class, and they need a set number of credits to graduate with a diploma.

title: Support for students learning English
text: Public schools must help students who are learning English, called English learners (ELs or ELLs). When you enroll, you will fill out a home language survey. If a language other than English is used at home, the school tests your child's English and, if needed, provides English language development services such as ESL classes or bilingual programs. These services are free. Federal law, including the Civil Rights Act and the Supreme Court case Lau v. Nichols, requires that English learners get real access to their education. Your child can leave the program once they pass an English proficiency test, and you can ask the school to explain the program options.

title: Special education, IEPs and 504 plans
text: If your child has a disability or you think they learn differently, you can ask the school in writing for a free evaluation. Under the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA), a child who qualifies gets an Individualized Education Program (IEP): a written plan with goals and services such as speech therapy or extra classroom support. A 504 plan, under Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act, gives accommodations like extra test time to students whose disability affects learning but who may not need specialized instruction. Parents are members of the IEP team, must give consent, and have the right to an interpreter at IEP meetings and to have documents explained in their language.

title: Your right to an interpreter and school communication
text: Schools must communicate important information to parents in a language they understand. This includes enrollment, report cards, discipline, special education, and parent-teacher conferences. You can ask for a free interpreter or translated documents, and the school should not ask your child or another student to interpret for you. Parent-teacher conferences usually happen once or twice a year and are a chance to hear how your child is doing and ask questions. You can also ask to meet the teacher at other times. Many schools use apps or email to send news, so tell the office which language you prefer.

title: Report cards and grades
text: Schools send report cards several times a year, often every quarter or trimester. Many middle and high schools use letter grades: A is excellent, B is good, C is average, D is barely passing, and F means failing. Some use percentages, and elementary schools often use numbers like 1 to 4 to show whether a child meets grade-level standards. High school grades are combined into a grade point average (GPA), usually on a 4.0 scale, which colleges look at. Many districts have an online parent portal where you can see grades, missing assignments and attendance at any time; ask the school office how to get a login.

title: Free and reduced-price school meals
text: Through the National School Lunch Program and School Breakfast Program, children from families with lower incomes can get free or reduced-price meals at school. Eligibility is based on household size and income, not immigration status, and using school meals does not count against families in immigration public charge decisions. You do not need a Social Security number for your child; on the application, the adult filling it out can mark that they do not have one. Some schools offer free meals to every student through the Community Eligibility Provision. Applications are available from the school office or district website and can be submitted at any time during the year.

title: Attendance and absences
text: Every state has compulsory attendance laws that require children to attend school, usually from about age 6 until 16 or 18 depending on the state. When your child is absent, contact the school the same day and give the reason, such as illness or a family emergency; schools may ask for a note. Too many unexcused absences can be considered truancy, which may lead to meetings with the school and, in some states, court involvement. Missing 10 percent or more of the school year, called chronic absenteeism, can hurt learning even if the absences are excused. If something is making it hard for your child to attend, ask the school counselor for help.
